intro: Every photo here is our own crew on a real Miami-Dade property — no stock imagery. Removals in tight side yards, canopies reduced properly rather than topped, palms cleared of dead fronds without stripping the crown, and storm debris chipped and hauled the same day. If you want to see something closer to your own property, call (305) 299-1189 and we will show you a job like it.

projects.title: Storm cleanup, chipped and hauled the same day
projects.alt: Crew feeding storm-felled branches into a chipper on a residential street while a bucket lift works the damaged tree behind
projects.description: Bucket lift working the damaged tree while the chipper runs on the street below. Chipping as we cut is what keeps a job like this to one day instead of leaving a pile at the kerb for the county to collect.

projects.title: Tight-access removal by tracked lift
projects.alt: Compact tracked spider lift set up in a narrow side yard beside a two-storey house to reach a large tree
projects.description: The tracked spider lift fits through a standard side gate and spreads its weight across the turf. It is what lets us reach trees behind a house without putting a truck on the lawn — or telling a customer the job cannot be done.

projects.title: Ficus reduced, not topped
projects.alt: Before and after of a large ficus, overgrown and shapeless on the left, reduced to a defined rounded canopy on the right
projects.description: A crown reduction taken back to laterals rather than cut to stubs. The tree keeps its structure, seals its wounds, and holds this shape for years instead of throwing out weak regrowth that needs re-cutting every season.

projects.title: Large removal, sectioned and lowered
projects.alt: Crew member beside a large tree cut down to two trunk sections, surrounded by the sectioned canopy laid out on the lawn
projects.description: Taken down in pieces and roped down rather than felled, because there was no direction this could safely have fallen. The canopy is laid out on the lawn ready to feed the chipper.

projects.title: Palm cluster cleared of dead fronds
projects.alt: Before and after of a cluster of palms, heavy with dead fronds on the left and cleanly trimmed on the right with a lift alongside
projects.description: Dead fronds and seed pods removed, live crowns left intact. The opposite of the 'hurricane cut' that strips a palm to a handful of uprights and leaves it weaker than it started.

projects.title: Date palm pruned to a clean crown
projects.alt: Before and after of a date palm, heavy with dead fronds on the left and pruned back to a clean crown on the right
projects.description: Correct palm work takes the dead material and nothing else. The fronds are how a palm feeds itself and how it buffers wind at the crown — removing healthy ones does not protect it.

projects.title: Coconut palm removal over a patio
projects.alt: Before and after of a coconut palm beside a house, standing on the left and fully removed with the debris stacked on the right
projects.description: Removed in sections directly over a covered patio, with the fronds and nuts cleared and the area swept before we left.

projects.title: Overgrowth cleared back to open ground
projects.alt: Before and after of an overgrown corner of a garden, dense vegetation on the left and cleared open ground on the right
projects.description: Roots taken out rather than cut to ground level. In South Florida that is the difference between clearing something and clearing it again next season.

projects.title: Mature live oak, thinned for storm season
projects.alt: Mature live oak with a wide spreading canopy over a suburban street, with a bucket truck parked alongside
projects.description: Selective thinning through the interior. The tree keeps its height, spread and shade, and wind moves through the canopy rather than loading the trunk and root plate.

projects.title: Routine palm maintenance from the ground
projects.alt: Tropical South crew member in a branded blue shirt using an extension pole saw on a palm beside a trimmed hedge
projects.description: Not everything needs a lift. A good share of routine palm maintenance is pole work — done properly, on a schedule, so it never becomes a bigger job.
